tldr: In robot navigation using world models, this paper proposes "Hydra," a discrete World Action Model that internalizes the planner inside the model and completes both candidate search and collision evaluation entirely within a discrete latent space. By eliminating image decoding through Discrete Latent Planning (DLP) and continuous Flow Matching execution, it speeds up planning by more than 500x compared to prior methods, demonstrating real-time obstacle avoidance and path tracking on physical robots.
hero_caption: Comparison between a conventional Navigation World Model (NWM, top) and the proposed Hydra (bottom). In NWM, an external planner blindly shoots samples in an unconstrained continuous space and decodes every candidate back to raw images for evaluation, which breaks computationally. In contrast, Hydra integrates the planner directly inside the model, conducting search and collision evaluation within a physically valid discrete latent manifold to achieve real-time decision-making in about 0.9 seconds.
overview:
In visual navigation where robots are guided purely by camera images, world models that imagine the consequences of actions are attracting high expectations. However, conventional world model planning has hit a major wall: generative models and external planners operate decoupled from each other. As a result, the planner must blindly sample trajectories from an unconstrained continuous space, and to check their validity, it has to decode every candidate back into high-dimensional raw images for evaluation. This incurs an enormous computational cost that simply cannot keep up with a physical robot's control loop.

To address this, the authors developed "Hydra," a discrete World Action Model that internalizes both the sampler and the evaluator directly inside the world model. By using early fusion across three modalities—visual states, physical poses, and control actions—Hydra establishes a unified latent manifold and compresses it into a discrete vocabulary of kinodynamic intents via Vector-Quantized (VQ) codebooks. This inherently eliminates the sampling of physically impossible, wasteful trajectories. Furthermore, candidate evaluation avoids decoding into image space altogether. Instead, it relies on a "Kinematic-Perceptual Cost (KPC)" that directly measures collision risk from quantization errors and prediction entropy within the discrete latent space. Only the single selected discrete intent is mapped back into smooth continuous control commands using conditional Flow Matching.

When evaluated on physical robots—a quadruped (Spot) and a wheeled robot (Jackal)—prior world model methods (NWM) failed, requiring over 500 seconds per planning cycle. In contrast, Hydra generated safe trajectories in approximately 0.9 seconds (a 500x+ speedup) and achieved high success rates in obstacle-cluttered environments. It also demonstrated equal or superior navigation stability compared to leading imitation learning baseline policies in local path tracking tasks.
contributions: Designed a World Action Model (WAM) with early fusion across visual states, poses, and actions, preserving physical consistency while keeping the model compact at 143M parameters.
Proposed Discrete Latent Planning (DLP), which avoids unconstrained continuous space search and instead efficiently searches and filters over a learned discrete intent codebook.
Constructed a Kinematic-Perceptual Cost (KPC) that detects collision risks purely from latent quantization errors and prediction entropy without decoding into image space.

Demonstrated on two physical robotic platforms (Spot and Jackal) that Hydra drastically outperforms prior world models in planning speed and matches or exceeds imitation learning models in real-world traversal performance.

sections.heading: Why Couldn't World Model Planning Run on Physical Robots?
sections.summary: Conventional navigation world models suffer from decoupled generative models and external planners, creating bottlenecks in reckless candidate sampling and heavy image-decoding evaluations. Hydra solves this by internalizing the planner into the model and finishing both search and evaluation entirely within a discrete latent space.
sections.details:
End-to-end reactive policies that map camera images directly to motor commands run smoothly in structured environments. However, because they lack an internal model to predict future physical consequences, they suffer from a fundamental weakness: they easily get stuck in local optima such as dead ends.

While world models (WMs) have gained traction to overcome this myopic behavior, conventional approaches like Navigation World Models (NWM) face a fatal "representation misalignment." The planners that generate and evaluate actions (such as CEM or MPPI) are decoupled from the generative model. Consequently, the planner is forced to blindly sample trajectories from a vast, unconstrained continuous space. On top of that, to judge whether a trajectory is good, each candidate's latent state must be decoded back into high-dimensional raw pixels and compared to the goal using perceptual metrics like LPIPS. This computational cost blows up, making it impossible to meet real-time robot control cycles.

Here is the key: Hydra embeds the planner itself (both generator and evaluator) right inside the world model. It trains visual states, physical robot poses, and control actions jointly from the start into a unified latent manifold. Then, using vector quantization (VQ), it compresses this continuous space into a vocabulary of physically executable kinodynamic intents (macro action primitives). This restricts planning search solely to a finite set of discrete codes known to be physically plausible.

The evaluation mechanism is equally innovative. When a candidate intent heads into an obstacle—representing an out-of-distribution (OOD) state—the quantization error against the VQ codebook surges, and prediction entropy spikes. Leveraging this property, the authors devised the "Kinematic-Perceptual Cost (KPC)," which directly scores safety within the latent space without decoding pixels. Only the best selected discrete intent is reconstructed into smooth real-world commands via continuous Flow Matching, enabling safe, high-speed planning.

captions.F1: Comparison of planning approaches in world models. In NWM (top), an external planner searches an unconstrained continuous space, yielding many invalid trajectories (red lines) and taking minutes for image decoding. In contrast, Hydra (bottom) searches only along a valid topological manifold inside the model (green lines) and completes planning in 0.9 seconds via latent-space evaluation.

sections.heading: Navigating the Gap Between Reactive Policies and Giant World Models
sections.summary: Prior robot navigation approaches are categorized across four perspectives: reactive policies, world models, model-based planning, and modality fusion methods. Hydra occupies a unique niche, achieving true discrete latent-space search within an edge-deployable, lightweight 143M-parameter footprint.
sections.details:
This paper clarifies Hydra's standing by categorizing related work into four lineages:

- Reactive navigation policies (ViNT, NoMaD, etc.): Strong action models trained on large datasets. However, because they are open-loop mappings that cannot forecast future environments, they cannot anticipate obstacles or dead ends to proactively correct and prune trajectories.
- Generative world models: Models that predict the future conditioned on actions. However, recent trends (such as DreamZero) push toward massive models with billions of parameters, where exploratory planning that demands multiple forward passes per step becomes computationally infeasible. Hydra is deliberately designed with a compact 143M parameters, targeting real-time search on robot edge compute.
- Model-based planning: MPPI and CEM in continuous spaces are notoriously sample-inefficient. Even in latent-space planning like JEPA-based methods, the action space itself remains continuous, leaving inefficiency unresolved. DreamerV3 and similar models handle discrete latent variables, but they do not integrate them with physical, real-time planning and safety cost functions on real robots. Hydra discretizes the representation itself and ranks candidates directly in the latent space.
- Early alignment vs. in-context alignment: Many recent foundation models (Cosmos, Gato, etc.) rely on in-context alignment, sequencing tokens of different modalities within a Transformer. However, self-attention must simultaneously resolve cross-modality alignment and temporal dynamics, ballooning model size and required training data. Following VertiFormer, Hydra adopts early fusion, adding and fusing visual, pose, and action tokens before feeding them to the sequence model. This lets the model focus purely on learning physical dynamics, preserving strong physical consistency even at a small model size.

sections.heading: Architecture: Discrete Latent Planning and Continuous Flow Matching
sections.summary: This section details Hydra's overall architecture and algorithm. It consists of multimodal representation learning via early fusion, discrete bottlenecks with asymmetric VQ codebooks, Kinematic-Perceptual Cost (KPC) without pixel reconstruction, and local path tracking under global guidance.
sections.details:
Hydra's architecture and algorithm are built upon four core components:

3.1 Navigation Formulation
Unlike reactive methods (direct observation-to-action) or world model approaches (predicting images from continuous actions for external evaluation), Hydra is formulated as a World Action Model (WAM). From observation history $\mathcal{H}_t=\{I_t, p_t, a_{t-1}\}$ (images, robot poses, and previous actions), it jointly predicts future visual states $\hat{I}$, poses $\hat{p}$, and actions $\hat{a}$. Predicting poses allows direct computation of geometric goal distances, predicting images forecasts collisions, and predicting actions drives the robot.

3.2 Unified Representation and Discrete Bottleneck
Visual features are extracted using a frozen VAE, while low-dimensional poses and actions are mapped using Fourier feature encodings. Early fusion sums these together into a single token stream. After compressing the context with a Transformer encoder, the decoder generates future intent tokens and passes them through modality-specific VQ codebooks. A key design choice here is an "asymmetric vocabulary size." While the visual head is allocated 2048 codes to maintain expressiveness, kinematic poses and actions receive small codebooks of just 64 codes each. This balances fast searchability with physical plausibility.

3.3 Discrete Latent Planning (DLP) and the KPC Cost
Candidate trajectories are searched over the learned codebook space. An unbiased prior generates an initial seed, and smooth Gumbel noise expands diverse path candidates. Candidates are then evaluated using the following Kinematic-Perceptual Cost $\mathcal{J}_{\text{KPC}}(\tau)$:
$$\mathcal{J}_{\text{KPC}}(\tau) = \sum_{k=1}^{H} \gamma^{k} \left( \lambda_{\text{geo}} \mathcal{C}_{\text{geo}} + \lambda_{\text{img}} \mathcal{C}_{\text{img}} + \lambda_{\text{prior}} \mathcal{C}_{\text{prior}} + \lambda_{\text{ent}} \mathcal{C}_{\text{ent}} + \lambda_{\text{vq}} \mathcal{C}_{\text{vq}} \right)$$
The geometric cost $\mathcal{C}_{\text{geo}}$ is the Euclidean distance between predicted poses and the goal. Crucially, the latter three terms handle collision avoidance: $\mathcal{C}_{\text{prior}}$ measures deviation from expert demonstrations, $\mathcal{C}_{\text{ent}}$ is the Shannon entropy of predicted visual tokens (prediction uncertainty), and $\mathcal{C}_{\text{vq}}$ is the quantization error (cosine distance) between continuous intents and the visual codebook. When the model tries to imagine a trajectory crashing into a wall or obstacle, quantization error and entropy spike dramatically because that state does not exist in the training distribution. In other words, danger is detected and pruned simply by observing latent space distortion without generating images. Finally, only the single best trajectory is decoded into continuous commands using Flow Matching and sent to the robot.

3.4 Local Path Following with Global Guidance
When subgoals are provided by a global planner like A*, Hydra functions as a local path-tracking policy. It offers two strategies: Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG), which interpolates between unconditional and goal-conditioned intents in latent space, and subgoal sampling, which samples valid candidates from the prior and ranks them by geometric distance.

sections.heading: Physical Robot Experiments: 500x Faster Planning and Safe Navigation
sections.summary: Real-world robot runs and offline validations were conducted using the Spot quadruped and Jackal wheeled robots. Hydra outperformed NWM in video generation consistency and achieved a 500x+ speedup over NWM in real-world planning, demonstrating high success rates.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated three core questions: long-horizon prediction consistency, real-time planning feasibility, and local tracking accuracy.

4.1 Grounded Generation and Long-Horizon Consistency
Autoregressive video generation was evaluated for 16 seconds (4 FPS, 64 frames total) using the RECON dataset. As shown in Table 1, Hydra outperformed NWM in Fréchet Video Distance (FVD). While continuous latent models like NWM accumulate errors and begin hallucinating actions after about 8 seconds, Hydra's discrete codebook preserves physical grounding, maintaining consistent, non-degrading predictions over the full 16 seconds.

4.2 Real-World Planning Performance
Using a Clearpath Jackal and a Boston Dynamics Spot, the authors conducted short-range navigation toward goals roughly 8 meters away. Baselines included the continuous models NWM and VertiFormer (MPPI).
The results were dramatic (Table 2). NWM, using CEM in continuous space, took over 500 seconds per planning cycle, completely breaking down for physical deployment. VertiFormer with MPPI ran in roughly 0.7 seconds, but lacking a structural prior, it produced reckless trajectories attempting to pass through obstacles, resulting in a 0% success rate in obstacle environments. In contrast, Hydra's DLP finished planning in about 0.9 seconds (over 500x faster than NWM), achieving a 10/10 success rate in clear environments and 8/10 in environments with obstacles and blind corners.

4.3 Latent Collision Detection Behavior
Analyzing behavior when driving the robot straight toward an obstacle revealed that visual codebook quantization error ($\mathcal{C}_{\text{vq}}$) and prediction entropy ($\mathcal{C}_{\text{ent}}$) surged in unison as the robot neared collision. The cost peaked right before the model would otherwise hallucinate a clear path, reliably eliminating dangerous candidates without pixel decoding.

4.4 Local Path Following Performance
Using Spot to follow waypoints from a global planner, Hydra was compared against reactive base policies (GNM, ViNT, NoMaD). While existing reactive models required high-frequency goal images at 2 Hz, Hydra achieved equal or higher success rates with sparse waypoint conditioning and required significantly fewer human interventions. CFG was fastest over short distances, while sampling was more stable over long distances, confirming the utility of both strategies.

4.5 Ablation Study
Ablations on KPC cost components revealed that when the goal is in a blind spot, disabling the image goal term $\mathcal{C}_{\text{img}}$ is essential (improving success from 20% to 80%). Removing any of $\mathcal{C}_{\text{prior}}$, $\mathcal{C}_{\text{vq}}$, or $\mathcal{C}_{\text{ent}}$ significantly worsened collision rates, proving each acts as an independent safety signal on both robotic platforms.

sections.heading: Emerging Challenges: Visual Complexity and Dynamic Obstacles
sections.summary: The paper candidly discusses three limitations: false positives in quantization-based collision detection, disappearance of dynamic objects like pedestrians, and the trade-off between expressiveness and inference latency.
sections.details:
Several challenges remain for Hydra's real-world deployment:

- Conflation of visual complexity with collision risk: While quantization error ($\mathcal{C}_{\text{vq}}$) is effective, it is not flawless. For instance, high-frequency, complex textures like tall grass or bushes are traversable, yet difficult for the codebook to reconstruct. This yields high error, leading to false-positive obstacle detections. Conversely, flat, featureless single-color walls are easy to reconstruct, creating a risk that true dangers might be underscored.
- Disappearance of dynamic agents: In crowded environments with pedestrians, individuals sometimes blended into the background and vanished. This stems from the relatively small visual codebook size (2048), which discards small objects as high-frequency noise, as well as the characteristics of the pretrained Stable Diffusion VAE.
- Expressiveness vs. latency trade-off: Generalizing to unseen environments requires expanding codebook vocabulary, but larger vocabularies increase nearest-neighbor search complexity, eroding real-time performance. Future work will require hierarchical codebooks or dynamic vocabulary adaptation.

sections.heading: Conclusion: The Significance of Discretizing Robot 'Intents'
sections.summary: Hydra achieves real-time physical robot control with a world model by integrating the planner internally and pairing discrete latent intents with Flow Matching. It demonstrates the profound effectiveness of discretizing physical dynamics for planning.
sections.details:
By combining an early fusion encoder with vector-quantized bottlenecks, Hydra successfully bridges the predictive power of generative world models with the real-time control loops of physical robots.

Formulating robot action intents as a discrete vocabulary and performing planning and safety evaluations directly in that latent space via Discrete Latent Planning (DLP) eliminates the massive overhead of continuous sampling and image decoding. Outperforming NWM and VertiFormer in planning speed and traversal reliability on physical robots strongly suggests that "intent discretization" is a compelling paradigm for future robotic foundation models.

sections.heading: Appendix: Training Stabilization and Two-Stage Exploration
sections.summary: The appendix details linear anchoring techniques to stably co-train discrete codebooks with continuous Flow Matching, as well as a two-stage stochastic exploration algorithm for generating diverse trajectory candidates.
sections.details:
Key insights from the appendix for understanding the methodology include:

- Physical Grounding via Unnormalized Actions: Standard foundation models (like GNM or ViNT) normalize actions by maximum platform velocity. However, this erases the distinction between a slow indoor cart and a fast all-terrain buggy. Hydra deliberately retains unnormalized, absolute action values. As a result, low-speed and high-speed maneuvers naturally cluster within the codebook, tightly linking visual context with physical velocity limits.
- Training Stabilization via Deterministic Linear Anchors: Passing a randomly initialized discrete codebook directly to a continuous ODE solver causes training to diverge. Hydra introduces a simple linear projection and MSE commitment loss (deterministic anchor) ahead of Flow Matching. While deep non-linear MLPs allow the codebook to collapse into lazy representations, strict linear projection forces high codebook utilization (perplexity increased from 465 to 608), forming a stable latent manifold.
- Two-Stage Noise Injection for Exploration: To sample diverse paths from the discrete codebook, search proceeds in two stages (Algorithm 1). In the first stage, temporally smoothed Gaussian noise is added to the continuous intent query before entering the Transformer decoder, producing fundamentally distinct trajectory branches (e.g., sharp right vs. left). In the second stage, temporally smoothed Gumbel noise is added to the codebook logits to sample fine-grained variations among Top-K candidates. This dual-noise design enables temporally smooth yet boldly exploratory trajectory proposals.

takeaways: In world model planning, internalizing the planner into the model and searching a discrete latent space is overwhelmingly more efficient than searching continuous spaces with external planners.
Monitoring VQ quantization error and prediction entropy in latent space detects collision risks with high accuracy and prunes unsafe trajectories without decoding back to raw pixels.
Training on unnormalized, absolute actions and poses rather than velocity-normalized values grounds the model in true physical scale and platform constraints.

A hybrid structure that decides broad macro-behaviors via discrete intents and decodes them into smooth control commands using continuous Flow Matching is exceptionally practical for physical robot control.
limitations: Visually complex textures like tall grass cannot be fully reconstructed by the codebook, leading to false positives where safe terrain is misclassified as an obstacle.
Due to the compact visual codebook vocabulary and VAE properties, dynamic agents like pedestrians can blur into the background and vanish, posing safety issues in crowds.

Expanding vocabulary size improves generalization but raises nearest-neighbor search latency, making the trade-off between expressiveness and real-time execution difficult to resolve with static codebooks alone.
